source_text:
Οὐδὲ γὰρ μόνον περὶ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐστὶν ἡ ἀμφισβήτησις, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τοῦ εἴδους αὐτοῦ τῆς νηστείας. οἱ μὲν γὰρ οἴονται μίαν ἡμέραν δεῖν αὐτοὺς νηστεύειν· οἱ δὲ δύο, οἱ δὲ καὶ πλείονας. οἱ δὲ τεσσαράκοντα ὥρας ἡμερινάς τε καὶ νυκτερινὰς συμμετροῦσι τὴν ἡμέραν αὐτῶν. (for. ut Vet. Interp. συμμετροῦντες, ὁρίζουσι τὴν ἡ. αὐ.) καὶ τοιαύτη μὲν ποικιλία τῶν ἐπιτηρούντων· οὐ νῦν ἐφ’ ἡμῶν γεγονυῖα, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολὺ πρότερον ἐπὶ τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν· τῶν παρὰ τὸ ἀκριβὲς ὡς εἰκὸς κρατούντων, τὴν καθ’ ἁπλότητα καὶ ἰδιωτισμὸν συνήθειαν εἰς τὸ μετέπειτα πεποιηκότων· καὶ οὐδὲν ἔλαττον πάντες οὗτοι εἰρήνευσάν τε, καὶ εἰρηνεύομεν πρὸς ἀλλήλους· καὶ ἡ διαφωνία τῆς νηστείας, τὴν ὁμόνοιαν τῆς πίστεως συνίστησι. Attulit hæc et proxime post ait: Τούτοις καὶ ἱστορίαν προστίθησιν (Irenæus) ἣν οἰκείως παραθήσομαι τοῦτον ἔχουσαν τὸν τρόπον.
Ἐν οἷς καὶ οἱ πρὸ Σωτῆρος πρεσβύτεροι οἱ προστάντες τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἧς σὺ νῦν ἀφηγῇ, Ἀνίκητον λέγομεν καὶ Πίον, Ὑγῖνόν τε καὶ Τελεσφόρον καὶ Ξύστον, οὔτε αὐτοὶ ἐτήρησαν, οὔτε τοῖς μετ’ αὐτῶν ἐπέτρεπον· καὶ οὐδὲν 10 ἔλαττον αὐτοὶ μὴ τηροῦντες, εἰρήνευον τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν παροικιῶν ἐν αἷς ἐτηρεῖτο ἐρχομένοις πρὸς αὐτούς. καί τοι μᾶλλον ἐναντίον ἦν τὸ τηρεῖν, τοῖς μὴ τηροῦσι. καὶ οὐδέ ποτε διὰ τὸ εἶδος τοῦτο ἀπεβλήθησαν τινές· ἀλλ’ αὐτοὶ μὴ τηροῦντες οἱ πρὸ σοῦ πρεσβύτεροι, τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν παροικιῶν τηροῦσιν ἔπεμπον εὐχαριστίαν. καὶ τοῦ μακαρίου Πολυκάρπου ἐπιδημήσαντος τῇ Ῥώμῃ ἐπὶ Ἀνικήτου· καὶ περὶ ἄλλων τινῶν μικρὰ σχόντες πρὸς ἀλλήλους, εὐθὺς εἰρήνευσαν· περὶ τούτου τοῦ κεφαλαίου μὴ φιλεριστήσαντες εἰς ἑαυτούς. οὔτε γὰρ ὁ Ἀνίκητος τὸν Πολύκαρπον πεῖσαι ἐδύνατο μὴ τηρεῖν, ἅτε μετὰ Ἰωάννου τοῦ μαθητοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀποστόλων οἷς συνδιέτριψεν, ἀεὶ τετηρηκότα· οὔτε μὴν ὁ Πολύκαρπος τὸν Ἀνίκητον ἔπεισε τηρεῖν, λέγοντα τὴν συνήθειαν τῶν πρὸ αὐτοῦ πρεσβυτέρων ὀφείλειν κατέχειν. καὶ τούτων οὕτως ἐχόντων, ἐκοινώνησαν ἑαυτοῖς· καὶ ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ παρεχώρησεν ὁ Ἀνίκητος τὴν εὐχαριστίαν τῷ Πολυκάρπῳ κατ’ ἐντροπὴν δηλονότι, καὶ μετ’ εἰρήνης ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων ἀπηλλάγησαν, πάσης τῆς ἐκκλησίας εἰρήνην ἐχόντων καὶ τῶν τηρούντων καὶ τῶν μὴ τηρούντων. Apud Eusebium ibidem.
thought_title: The Paschal fast dispute is old and does not break unity
orientation: Irenaeus is writing to Victor of Rome, arguing that disagreement over the day and manner of the Paschal fast has existed long before them and has never broken the peace between churches.
pass_a_gloss: For not only about the day is the dispute, but also about the manner itself of the fast. For some think that they must fast one day; others two, others also more. Others measure their day as forty hours, daytime and nighttime. And such variety of those observing; not now in our time having come about, but also much earlier among those before us; of those holding to what is not exact, as is likely, having made the custom in simplicity and plainness into the time afterward; and no less all these both kept peace, and we keep peace with one another; and the disagreement of the fast confirms the unity of faith. To these he also adds a history which I will set out fittingly, having this manner. Among whom also the bishops before Soter, who presided over the church which you now lead, Anicetus we mean and Pius, Hyginus and Telesphorus and Xystus, neither did they themselves observe, nor did they permit those with them; and no less they themselves not observing, kept peace with those coming to them from the local churches in which it was observed. And yet rather contrary was the observing, to those not observing. And never because of this manner were any cast out; but they themselves not observing, the bishops before you, sent the Eucharist to those from the local churches observing. And when the blessed Polycarp visited Rome under Anicetus; and about some other small matters having had differences with one another, immediately they made peace; about this main point not having quarreled with each other. For neither was Anicetus able to persuade Polycarp not to observe, since with John the disciple of our Lord, and the remaining apostles with whom he spent time, he had always observed; nor indeed did Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe, who said that he ought to hold the custom of the bishops before him. And these things being so, they shared communion with one another; and in the church Anicetus yielded the Eucharist to Polycarp out of respect clearly, and with peace they departed from one another, all the church having peace, both those observing and those not observing.

pass_b_english: For the dispute is not only about the day, but also about the very manner of the fast. Some think they should fast one day, some two, some even more; others measure their day as forty hours of daytime and nighttime together. And this variety among those who observe the fast did not arise in our time, but long before us, among those who came before us—those who, as is likely, held to what was not exact and passed on the custom in its plainness and simplicity to those after them. And none the less, all of these kept peace, and we keep peace with one another; and the disagreement over the fast confirms the unity of faith.

Among these were the bishops before Soter who presided over the church which you now lead—I mean Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Xystus. They neither observed the fast themselves nor permitted those with them to observe it, and none the less, though they did not observe it, they kept peace with those who came to them from the local churches where it was observed. And yet observing the fast was all the more opposed to those who did not observe it. And no one was ever cast out because of this manner of the fast; rather, the bishops before you, though they did not observe it, sent the Eucharist to those from the local churches who did observe it.

And when the blessed Polycarp visited Rome in the time of Anicetus, though they had some small disagreements with one another about other matters, they immediately made peace, not being eager to quarrel with one another over this point. For neither could Anicetus persuade Polycarp not to observe the fast, since Polycarp had always observed it with John the disciple of our Lord and the rest of the apostles with whom he had associated; nor could Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe it, since Anicetus said he was bound to hold to the custom of the bishops before him. And since matters stood thus, they shared communion with one another; and in the church Anicetus yielded the Eucharist to Polycarp, clearly out of respect, and they parted from one another in peace, with the whole church—both those who observed the fast and those who did not—holding peace.
notes: The source text contains a Latin editorial insertion: '(for. ut Vet. Interp. συμμετροῦντες, ὁρίζουσι τὴν ἡ. αὐ.)' indicating a variant reading from an old interpretation, and 'Attulit hæc et proxime post ait:' and 'Apud Eusebium ibidem.' which are Eusebius's framing comments, not part of Irenaeus's letter.

problems.quote: the day and manner of the Paschal fast
problems.why: The intro introduces 'Paschal fast' but section 1 uses only 'the fast' or 'it', never repeating 'Paschal'. A reader may forget what fast is meant.
problems.fix: Add 'Paschal' at least once in section 1.

problems.why: 'Local churches' means Asian congregations, but 'the church' shifts between Rome and universal church; reader may lose track.
problems.fix: Clarify 'the church in Rome' vs 'churches in Asia'.

variants.text: the church which you now lead

problems.quote: And yet observing the fast was all the more opposed to those who did not observe it.
problems.why: Contradicts the argument; should mean the fast was 'not opposed' or 'tolerated', not 'all the more opposed'.

problems.quote: held to what was not exact
problems.why: 'Not exact' is vague; seems to mean they held to a tradition that was not precise/rigorous, but could misread as 'inaccurate'.

edits.old: And yet observing the fast was all the more opposed to those who did not observe it.
edits.new: And yet observing the fast was rather contrary to those who did not observe it.

edits.old: those who, as is likely, held to what was not exact and passed on the custom in its plainness and simplicity to those after them
edits.new: those who, as is likely, held to what was not exacting and passed on the custom in its plainness and simplicity to those after them

edits.old: For the dispute is not only about the day, but also about the very manner of the fast.
edits.new: For the dispute is not only about the day, but also about the very manner of the Paschal fast.

edits.old: they kept peace with those who came to them from the local churches where it was observed
edits.new: they kept peace with those who came to them from the churches in Asia where it was observed

fixed: Added 'Paschal' to the first mention of the fast in section 1, since the source's νηστεία refers to the Paschal fast and the brief's glossary sense confirms this; the English previously never repeated 'Paschal' after the title.

Changed 'all the more opposed' to 'rather contrary' to match the source's μᾶλλον ἐναντίον ἦν, which means 'was rather contrary' (i.e., the observing was contrary to the non-observing, but they still kept peace), not 'all the more opposed'.
Changed 'not exact' to 'not exacting' to match the source's παρὰ τὸ ἀκριβὲς, which means 'not exacting/rigorous' (i.e., not strict about the precise form), not 'inaccurate'.

Clarified 'the local churches' as 'the churches in Asia' to match the source's παροικίαι, which the brief glosses as local churches where the Asian custom was observed; this distinguishes them from the Roman church.
